<reason>Both sides argued at a high level with vivid framing and no fake sourcing. PRO's live route was strong: cities already engineer the funnel, visitors you accept must stand somewhere, and the "leak" means outward spread is already happening without rules, so an official, revocable map beats an informal one. Its refrain ("volume says how many, geography says who pays") was memorable and forced CON to answer allocation, not just volume. But CON built the harder-to-dislodge structure. Three arguments survived the exchange: (1) non-linear damage — adding load to a block already past its tipping point inflicts little marginal harm, while the same load pushes many un-tipped streets toward their line; (2) the choke-point vs capillary enforcement distinction, which directly and cleanly answered PRO's sharpest pressure question ("why does enforcement work only as a funnel?") rather than dodging it; (3) irreversibility — listings, algorithms and sunk hotel/conversion capital do not expire even if permits and posters do, which blunted PRO's "licenses expire" undo mechanism. CON also converted PRO's own concessions: the "cap volume if you must" line and the admission that naming a number "would be theatre" were turned into "the cap is rhetoric, the map is the policy." CON's answer to "where do they stand?" (the core has hardened plazas, transit interchange, sewers and tourism-employed staff; a residential street has a corner shop and a stairwell) was the most concrete moment in the debate. PRO's rejoinder that leftover bakeries and families "do not count as zero" was fair but conceded the mechanism, and CON's closing correctly reframed the comparison as marginal uncertain gain in an already-tipped district versus first-time loss in un-tipped ones. Minor execution cost to CON for the clipped over-length opening; not enough to offset. CON made the decision easier to reach.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's answer to PRO's pressure question on enforcement: distinguishing choke-point regulation (berth caps, bed licences — few actors, checkable at a gate) from capillary regulation (keeping a bakery a bakery across two hundred blocks, thousands of invisible private actors). It explained why overload is evidence against PRO's plan specifically rather than against CON's tools, and it neutralized PRO's central "your own tools work on a map" move.</best_rebuttal>
